subtype: Approach: avoiding the issue and building resentment [Pitfall]
passage: As the daughter-in-law, I never told my husband Jagdish's parents that their unannounced visits drained me. I smiled, put the kettle on, and cancelled my plans, again and again. Each time the doorbell rang without a call, my jaw tightened. I told myself it was not worth a fuss. Then one Saturday his mother said, lightly, that the curtains looked dusty. I heard myself shouting that nobody in this house ever asked whether I wanted guests, and that I was tired of being on show. The room went silent. Jagdish stared at his plate. His mother left in tears before tea. The curtains were never the problem, and now everyone was hurt over words I had let pile up for a year. I wish I had spoken up on the first Sunday. - Kiran

qa.q: What did Jagdish's mother say that set off the outburst?
qa.a: She said, lightly, that the curtains looked dusty.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling in the year before the outburst?
qa.a: Kiran felt drained and resentful, shown by the tightening jaw whenever the doorbell rang without a call.

qa.q: What could Kiran have done early on?
qa.a: Kiran could have said kindly, after the first surprise visit, that a call beforehand would help with planning, so the matter stayed small.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's mother have experienced the outburst?
qa.a: Jagdish's mother may have felt hurt and confused, since a light remark about curtains brought out a year of anger she had not known about.

grounding: Kiran stays silent about the unannounced visits until resentment explodes over a small comment.
